title: The Lost Art of Doubles: Why Tennis's Team Game Deserves More Attention
summary: In the age of singles superstars, doubles tennis is often treated as an afterthought. But the team format offers something the solo game cannot — genuine partnership under pressure. We make the case for doubles.
content:
When the great doubles partnerships are discussed — Woodbridge and Woodforde, the Bryan brothers, Nestor and Zimonjic — they are usually discussed in a separate conversation from the one about tennis's greatest players. The sport compartmentalises its formats. Singles is the main event. Doubles is the support act. Grand Slam coverage reflects this hierarchy: the men's singles final is prime time, the doubles final is a daytime slot on a secondary court.

This is a mistake. Doubles tennis, played at the highest level, is a different sport from singles — different skills, different tactics, different physical demands — and it is a compelling one. The case for giving it more attention is not sentimental. It is about what the format actually contains.

What Doubles Demands

At the net in doubles, the margins are measured in fractions of a second. The serve-and-volley combination — a serve that sets up a first volley that is then put away by a partner covering the net — requires coordination and timing that singles never demands. The ability to read your partner's intentions, to anticipate where the return is going, to cover the right court at the right moment, is a form of tennis intelligence that is entirely separate from the individual brilliance that singles rewards.

Communication under pressure — the signals that doubles partners use to coordinate tactics between points, the ability to read a partner's body language when things are going wrong, the trust that allows both players to commit fully to a tactic knowing the other will execute their part — these qualities are invisible on television but fundamental to elite doubles performance.

The Bryan Brothers and What They Showed

Bob and Mike Bryan, the American twin brothers who dominated professional doubles for the better part of two decades, demonstrated what a truly great doubles partnership looks like. Their record — Grand Slam titles in double figures, more weeks at number one than any other pair in history — was built on an almost supernatural coordination. They had played together since childhood. They knew each other's games completely.

What the Bryans showed was that doubles excellence, like singles excellence, requires dedicated development. Players who treat doubles as a secondary priority never reach the level of those who make it their focus. The skills are specific and must be specifically trained.

People watch doubles and they think it looks easy because we make it look smooth. The truth is that the smooth moments come from thousands of repetitions, from knowing exactly what my partner will do, from trusting each other completely. That takes years to build. It is anything but easy.

Why Singles Players Need Doubles

The tactical education that doubles provides — net positioning, volleys, the ability to construct a point from an aggressive first-strike mindset — has historically been reflected in singles players who play doubles seriously. Players who feel comfortable at the net, who can serve-and-volley, who understand the geometry of court coverage, have advantages at the net that purely baseline players lack.

The modern tendency toward baseline rallying in singles has reduced the tactical diversity of the game. Reintegrating doubles as a serious developmental priority might partially reverse that — producing singles players who are more complete, more comfortable in more situations, more difficult to pattern-beat.

What It Would Take

Giving doubles the attention it deserves would require broadcast decisions — better scheduling, better commentary, better camera work that communicates the positioning and tactical decisions that make the format interesting. It would require tournament scheduling that did not use doubles primarily as a time-filler. And it would require the sport's storytellers — journalists, broadcasters, social media producers — to tell doubles stories with the same investment they bring to singles.

None of this is impossible. The format deserves the effort.
author: SportsKeen Editorial
